doc.title: Rob Mounsey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 9, 2025

title: Playing the piano solo on Steely Dan's 'Glamour Profession'
summary: His only soloist role for Steely Dan, at Automated Beat around 1982, and how he found a comping part by playing on beat three-and.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Can you recall a studio date, a keyboard date where you came in and said to yourself, “Wow I’m not — this is going to be a real challenge for me” for one reason or another?
Yeah. Well my favorite story about that is the Steely Dan track called “Glamour Profession” where I played a piano solo. This is the only time that I was ever a soloist for them.
I don’t know Steely Dan fanatics know this, this is a famous thing. And you’re not one of them I sense. But anyway —
Well I am except that what you played I couldn’t hear because the Zoom —
Oh because Zoom cut it out.
Yes Zoom doesn’t really like it, but yes I’m a huge Steely Dan fan, yeah.

Well there’s a piano solo and they called me in to play the piano solo. This was Automated Beat in New York. It must have been 1982 I think. And you know they were famously, famously very, very exacting which nobody ever minded because everybody loved the music and loved the songs. And we got the piano solo in a couple of hours, maybe two hours, which is pretty good for them. Two punches, it’s 12 bars, we carefully made that. And then to my surprise Donald Fagen said, “And now we just need you to

just play, comp a little bit through the rest of the track because we don’t want the piano to just appear out of nowhere, we want it to kind of be part of the band so just —.” Okay that didn’t sound too difficult so they played the track and the song, if you remember it, is very harmonically strange. It’s very harmonically unsettled. It’s sort of constantly making left turns.
That’s a great word for it, I’ve never been able to pin down how that song makes me feel and you just did it. Unsettled.

Yeah. It’s harmonically, harmonically it sort of doesn’t come to rest. Where you think it’s coming to rest and then it jumps off and goes somewhere else. And so that was strange. But I mean if you’re just reading chord symbols and just kind of comping that shouldn’t be a problem. And yet they rolled the track and I tried to just you know play a rhythm comping part in whatever way felt natural at the time. I couldn’t find it because the track sounded so complete. I might have been the very last thing to be added to it. And the track sounded really finished and it felt finished and I couldn’t, whatever I played rhythmically, everybody was basically rhythmically playing a one-bar pattern. Not two or four, one. And whenever I played I felt like I was stepping on somebody else. So I had to go into the booth and say let me just really listen to the track and I had to try to listen really analytically. Like who’s playing what? Who’s playing on what beats of the bar? And what I came up with was nobody was really playing right on beat three except the kick drum, and there’s a very simple drum pattern. It’s got a [scats] like a, just quarter notes. But aside from the kick drum nobody was really playing right on beat three. So I went back out in the room and tried just playing on beat three for a minute, and ended up feeling like three-and. It goes one, two, three-and; one, two, three-and, and that started to feel strange but it started to feel good actually. So if you listen to that track now you’ll hear a lot of the track is the piano will just sort of play two eighth notes on the third beat. And it’s weird but it kind of worked and it sort of added to the personality of the song. You know it added to this kind of little bit like reggae-disco feeling of the song. And then there are a few other little things, a couple little decorations here and there. So that was a challenge and it wasn’t a challenge because it was difficult in any technical way, it was a challenge to figure out what would work.
